title: The Research Paper
bigQuestion: How does a writer turn one honest question into a long argument that other people can check?

story.title: Twelve Sources for One Street
story.kicker: A senior asks why a Chicago neighborhood kept a Czech name after most of the Czech families left, and the answer is not in any one place.
paragraphs: Dani grew up on Eighteenth Street in Pilsen. She knew the murals, the bakeries and the sound of the Pink Line. What she did not know, until a teacher asked, was why her neighborhood carried the name of a city in Bohemia. Pilsen is named for Plzen, a city in what is now the Czech Republic. Czech immigrants settled the area in the 1800s. By the time Dani was born, most of her neighbors were Mexican American. The name stayed. Why?

Her first stop was a search engine, and it gave her a paragraph. The paragraph said that Czech immigrants came, then Mexican families came, and the name remained. That was true, and it was useless, because it did not answer her question. It only restated it. A research question that can be answered in one paragraph was never a real research question. Dani wanted to know how a name survives a change of people, and who decided it should.

So she started collecting. The Encyclopedia of Chicago gave her the outline of the Czech years. A digitized newspaper from the 1970s showed a church still holding services in Czech while the parish school taught in Spanish. A university press book on Mexican Chicago explained how families moved west from the Near West Side when a highway and a campus were built. An oral history recorded a woman who had lived on the same block for sixty years. Each source knew one piece. None knew the whole.

By the end of the month Dani had twelve sources, a folder of notes and a question that had changed shape. She no longer asked why the name stayed. She asked what the name had come to mean to the people who lived under it, and how a neighborhood can hold two histories at once without erasing either. That question could carry a semester. It could carry twelve pages. Her sources disagreed with each other in places, and the disagreements were where her own argument began.

This chapter walks through what Dani did, step by step: how to choose a question that is big enough, how to find sources that can bear weight, how to read pages that fight back, how to build a long argument out of many voices, how to give every voice its proper credit, and how to revise until a stranger can follow you from the first line to the last.
story.think: Dani's first search gave her a true paragraph that answered nothing. What is the difference between a fact about a subject and an answer to a question about it?

lessons.title: A Question Worth a Semester
lessons.mainIdea: A strong research question is open, specific and arguable, and it cannot be settled by a single lookup.
reading: Compare two questions. First: When was the Chicago River reversed? Second: Why did Chicago decide that reversing a river was cheaper than cleaning its water, and who paid the cost downstream? The first has an answer you can look up in ten seconds: the main channel opened in 1900. The second could fill a semester. It asks about causes, choices and consequences, and thoughtful people could answer it differently. That difference is the whole test of a *research question*.

A workable research question has three traits. It is *open*: it cannot be answered yes or no, and it cannot be answered by one source. It is *specific*: it names a place, a time, a group or a text, so you know where to look. And it is *arguable*: a careful reader could reasonably reach a different conclusion, which means your paper will have to persuade rather than merely report. A question that is open but not specific, such as Why do cities change?, will drown you. A question that is specific but not arguable, such as How many people lived in Pilsen in 1920?, will bore you and your reader.

Most good questions start as bad ones and get better. Dani began with Why did the name stay? and found that the answer was too simple. She narrowed to one neighborhood, widened to two communities, and shifted from why to what it came to mean. Expect this. Write your first question down, try to answer it in one sentence, and notice what that sentence leaves out. The gap is your real question. Revise the question every time your reading shows you that you were asking the wrong thing.

One practical check before you commit: can you name two sources, right now, that would disagree about your question? If every source you can imagine would say the same thing, you have a report topic, not a research question. Disagreement is not a problem to avoid. It is the raw material of an argument. The paper you will write is your reasoned answer, set against the answers of others.

words.d: the open, specific, arguable question a research paper sets out to answer
of a question: unable to be answered yes or no, or by a single source
of a question: tied to a named place, time, group or text, so you know where to look
of a question or claim: something a careful reader could reasonably see differently

look.title: Three Drafts of One Question
look.text: Draft 1: Is social media bad for teenagers? Draft 2: How does social media affect teenagers? Draft 3: How has the shift from public posting to private group chats since 2015 changed how high school students handle conflict with friends?
look.prompt: Which of the three traits (open, specific, arguable) does each draft have, and which does it lack?

check.q: Which question is the best research question?
choices: Why did Chicago choose to reverse its river instead of cleaning its water, and who bore the cost?
In what year did the main channel of the reversed Chicago River open?
Is pollution bad?
How long is the Chicago River?
check.why: It is open, specific to a place and event, and arguable; the others are lookups or a yes-or-no question.

check.q: A question is open but not specific, such as Why do cities change? What does the lesson say will happen?
choices: It will bore the reader.
It will drown the writer, because there is nowhere to start looking.
It will be too easy to answer.
It cannot be answered at all.
check.why: Without a named place, time or group, the writer has no way to limit the search.

check.q: The lesson says to ask whether two sources would disagree about your question. Why?
choices: To prove the question is too hard.
To find sources you can copy from.
Because disagreement is the raw material of an argument; agreement means you have a report topic.
Because teachers require two sources.
check.why: If every source agrees, there is nothing to argue; the paper would only report.

lessons.title: Making a Research Plan
lessons.mainIdea: A research plan turns a big question into a calendar of small tasks, and it fixes deadlines for reading, drafting and revising before you begin.
reading: Here is the plan Dani wrote on a single page. Week 1: settle the question and list ten possible sources. Week 2: read and take notes on the four sources that seem strongest. Week 3: read six more, write a one-page summary of what the sources agree and disagree about. Week 4: outline. Weeks 5 and 6: draft the body. Week 7: draft the opening and ending, build the Works Cited list. Week 8: trade drafts with a reader, revise, proofread, submit. She taped it above her desk. That page is a *research plan*.

The plan works because it breaks one enormous task into pieces small enough to finish in a sitting. Nobody can write a research paper. People can find a source, read a chapter, write a paragraph. A plan also protects the part of the process that students most often skip: revision. When drafting slides into the last week, revision gets an hour at midnight. When the plan gives revision a full week, the paper gets a real second draft. Put the deadlines for the final stages on the calendar first, then work backward.

Your plan should list sub-questions as well as dates. Dani's big question about what the name of Pilsen came to mean broke into smaller ones: Who first used the name, and when? When did Mexican families begin arriving, and why there? Did anyone try to rename the neighborhood? How do current residents talk about the name? Each *sub-question* points toward a different kind of source. The first wants an encyclopedia and old maps. The last wants interviews and recent journalism. Listing them shows you what to search for.

Plans change, and that is fine. If a source you counted on turns out to be unavailable, or a sub-question turns out to be unanswerable, adjust the plan and keep going. What you should not change is the total time. A plan that keeps getting extended is not a plan. Keep a short *research log*: the date, what you looked at, what you found, what you will try next. Ten minutes of logging saves hours of retracing your steps when you need to cite a source you half remember.

words.d: a schedule that breaks a long project into dated tasks: question, sources, notes, outline, draft, revision
a smaller question inside the main one; each points toward a particular kind of source
a running record of what you searched, what you found and what you will try next

look.title: One Eight-Week Plan
look.cite: Dani's plan, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Reading and drafting get five of the eight weeks. What would go wrong if drafting started in week two?

check.q: Why does the lesson say to put the deadlines for the final stages on the calendar first?
choices: Because the ending of a paper is the hardest part to write.
Because teachers grade the ending most heavily.
Because sources are easier to find at the end.
So that revision keeps its full week instead of getting squeezed into the last night.
check.why: When drafting slides late, revision is what gets cut; fixing its dates first protects it.

check.q: Dani's sub-question 'How do current residents talk about the name?' points toward what kind of source?
choices: Interviews and recent journalism
Old maps
A nineteenth-century encyclopedia
A dictionary
check.why: Current attitudes are found in interviews and recent reporting, not in historical reference works.

check.q: What does the lesson say a plan that keeps getting extended is?
choices: A sign of thorough research
Not a plan
Normal for long papers
A reason to change the question
check.why: Plans may shift inside the total time, but the total time itself should not keep growing.

lessons.title: Scholarly Sources and Databases
lessons.mainIdea: Scholarly sources are written by experts, checked by other experts and found mostly through library databases rather than open web searches.
reading: Two articles about the same neighborhood. The first is a blog post with no author's name, no date and no list of where its facts came from. The second appeared in a university journal, names two historians as authors, was read and approved by other historians before it was printed, and ends with three pages of notes showing every source. The second is a *scholarly source*. The first might be right, but you have no way to check, and a research paper is built on things a reader can check.

The checking process is called *peer review*: before a journal prints an article, other experts in the field read it and can send it back for correction. Peer review does not guarantee truth, but it catches many errors and forces the writer to show evidence. Scholarly books from university presses go through a similar review. Newspapers of record, government reports and reference works such as the Encyclopedia of Chicago are not peer reviewed in the same way, but they have editors and standards, and they are appropriate for many questions. A personal website usually has neither.

Most scholarly articles do not turn up in an ordinary web search, or they turn up behind a paywall. They live in *databases*: searchable collections that libraries pay for. Google Scholar indexes many of them for free and often links to a readable copy. JSTOR holds decades of journal articles in history, literature and the social sciences. Public library systems, including the Chicago Public Library, give cardholders free access to research databases from home. Ask a librarian which databases fit your subject. Librarians are trained researchers, and helping you search is their job.

Searching a database is different from searching the web. Use fewer words and more precise ones. Dani's first search, Pilsen history, returned thousands of results. Her better search, Pilsen Chicago Czech Mexican, returned dozens. Adding a date range narrowed it further. Read the *abstract*, the short summary at the top of an article, before you download anything. Then check the article's own list of sources: an article's bibliography is a map to a dozen more sources, already vetted by an expert.

words.d: a book or article written by experts, reviewed by other experts, with full notes showing its sources
the process in which other experts read and approve an article before a journal publishes it
a searchable collection of articles, books or records, usually reached through a library
the short summary printed at the start of a scholarly article

look.title: Five Results, One Search
look.text: A search returns: (1) a peer-reviewed journal article from 2011; (2) a Chicago Tribune feature from 1978; (3) an anonymous blog post with no date; (4) an entry in the Encyclopedia of Chicago; (5) a comment on a video. A student needs to explain when Mexican families began arriving in Pilsen and why.
look.prompt: Rank the five for this question, and say what each one could and could not be trusted to tell you.

check.q: What does peer review do?
choices: Guarantees that an article is true
Makes an article free to read online
Has other experts read and approve an article before it is published, catching many errors
Adds an abstract to the article
check.why: Peer review is expert checking before publication; it reduces errors but does not guarantee truth.

check.q: Why does the lesson recommend reading an article's own list of sources?
choices: To count how many the author used
To check whether the article is long enough
To copy the list into your own paper
Because it is a map to more sources an expert has already vetted
check.why: A scholarly bibliography leads to further reliable sources on the same question.

check.q: Dani's search 'Pilsen history' returned thousands of results. What fixed it?
choices: Using more precise words and a date range
Searching the open web instead
Removing the word Pilsen
Downloading every result
check.why: Databases reward fewer, more exact terms and limits such as date ranges.

lessons.title: Reading Sources That Fight Back
lessons.mainIdea: Difficult scholarly texts are read in passes: first for the shape of the argument, then for the parts that answer your question, then closely.
reading: The first paragraph of the journal article ran two hundred words, used the phrase spatial assimilation twice, and cited six other scholars in parentheses. Dani read it three times and understood nothing. This is normal. Scholarly writing is written for other scholars, who already know the vocabulary and the earlier arguments. You are joining a conversation partway through. The fix is not to read harder. It is to read differently.

Read in passes. On the first pass, do not read the article at all; read around it. Read the abstract, the headings, the first sentence of each paragraph and the conclusion. Ask one question: what is this writer claiming? Write the answer in one sentence of your own. This is *skimming* with a purpose. On the second pass, find the two or three sections that touch your sub-questions and read those slowly, with a pencil. Skip the rest for now. On the third pass, if the article matters, read the whole thing, now that you know where it is going.

When a sentence will not open, take it apart. Find the main verb, then the subject. Put the parentheses and the long noun phrases aside for a moment. Spatial assimilation, in a sentence about immigrants, turns out to mean moving from an ethnic neighborhood into a mixed one as families earn more. Look up terms in the article's own definitions first, since scholars often define their key words in the opening pages. Keep a running *glossary* of the field's vocabulary in your log, in your own plain words.

Take notes that separate what the source says from what you think about it. A simple method: one column for the writer's claim and evidence, with page numbers, and a second column for your reaction, your questions and the connections to your other sources. Write the page number every single time. A paraphrase without a page number is a citation you will spend an hour reconstructing later. And write the note in your own words the first time, unless you are copying an exact quotation inside quotation marks. That habit will protect your integrity when you draft.

words.d: reading the abstract, headings, first sentences and conclusion to learn a text's shape before reading it closely
a list of a field's special terms with their meanings, kept in your own words
restating a source's idea entirely in your own words and sentence structure, with a citation

look.title: Bacon on Three Ways to Read
look.text: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested; that is, some books are to be read only in parts; others to be read, but not curiously; and some few to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention.
look.prompt: Match Bacon's three ways of reading to the three passes in this lesson. Which sources in a research project deserve to be chewed and digested?

check.q: On the first pass through a difficult article, what does the lesson say to read?
choices: Every sentence, slowly
The abstract, headings, first sentences and conclusion
Only the footnotes
The middle section
check.why: The first pass is for the shape of the argument, not the details.

check.q: Why does the lesson insist on writing the page number with every note?
choices: Teachers count page numbers
Page numbers prove you read the whole article
A note without a page number becomes a citation you must later spend time reconstructing
Databases require them
check.why: Citations need page numbers, and finding them again later wastes time.

check.q: What is the safest note-taking habit for later academic integrity?
choices: Copy long passages so you have the exact words
Take no notes and rely on memory
Note only your own opinions
Write notes in your own words, and put exact copied words inside quotation marks
check.why: Separating your words from the source's words at the note stage prevents accidental plagiarism in the draft.

lessons.title: Synthesis Across Sources
lessons.mainIdea: Synthesis means placing sources in conversation with each other, organized by idea rather than by source, so your own claim can emerge from their agreements and conflicts.
reading: A weak research paper marches through its sources one at a time: first what Author A said, then what Author B said, then C. That is a book report stacked twelve high. A strong paper is organized by *ideas*, and under each idea it brings in whichever sources speak to it, letting them agree, disagree and correct one another. Turning a pile of sources into that kind of conversation is *synthesis*.

The tool for synthesis is a grid. Down the side, list your sub-questions or themes. Across the top, list your sources. In each box, write in a few words what that source says about that theme, with a page number. Dani's grid had a row called reasons for moving to Pilsen. The university press book said highway and campus construction pushed families out of the Near West Side in the 1960s. The oral history said her interviewee followed a cousin who had found work nearby. The newspaper said cheap rent. The three do not contradict each other, but each alone would have been incomplete. The row, read across, became a paragraph.

Watch especially for the boxes where sources conflict. One of Dani's sources described the change in Pilsen as a smooth handoff between communities; another described tension over church buildings and school language. Conflict between sources is not a problem to hide. It is a place where you must decide, using evidence, which account is better supported, or explain how both could be partly right. Your judgment in those places is the *original contribution* of your paper. Anyone can summarize twelve sources. Only you can weigh them.

When the grid is full, read it row by row and write one sentence per row stating what the sources together show. Those sentences are the first draft of your outline. Then read the column of your own reactions and ask what claim they add up to. Dani's claim became this: the name Pilsen survived not because anyone chose it but because each community found reasons to keep it, and those reasons were different. Every row of the grid fed that sentence. That is what a thesis built by synthesis looks like.

words.d: combining several sources by idea so they answer a question together, revealing agreements, conflicts and gaps
the part of a paper that is the writer's own judgment: how sources are weighed and what they add up to
the one-sentence claim a whole paper argues for

look.title: One Row of Dani's Grid
rows: Sources citing family or work networks
Sources citing church or school ties
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the sample grid
look.prompt: Some sources appear in more than one row. If you were writing the paragraph on why families moved to Pilsen, which reasons would you lead with and why?

check.q: What is wrong with a paper that summarizes Author A, then Author B, then Author C?
choices: It is organized by source instead of by idea, so the sources never speak to each other.
It uses too many sources.
It has no citations.
It is too short.
check.why: Synthesis organizes by theme; a source-by-source march is a stack of reports.

check.q: According to the lesson, where does a paper's original contribution mostly come from?
choices: From finding a source nobody else has used
From the writer's judgment where sources conflict
From the length of the bibliography
From the formatting
check.why: Weighing conflicting accounts with evidence is the work only the writer can do.

check.q: In the synthesis grid, what goes across the top and down the side?
choices: Dates across the top, quotes down the side
Page numbers across the top, authors down the side
Sources across the top, themes or sub-questions down the side
Themes across the top, dates down the side
check.why: Each box then shows what one source says about one theme.

lessons.title: Organizing a Long Argument
lessons.mainIdea: A long argument holds together when each section answers one sub-question, the sections are ordered by logic, and every part points back to the thesis.
reading: A twelve-page paper is not a five-paragraph essay stretched thin. It is a building with rooms. Each room, usually a section with its own heading, takes up one sub-question and answers it. The reader should be able to enter any room and know what it is for. When Dani outlined, she wrote her thesis at the top of the page and then listed five sections: the Czech naming, the arrival of Mexican families, the years of overlap, the disputes, and what the name means now. Each section was a room, and each got a one-sentence job description.

Order the rooms by logic, not by the order you found things. Common orders: *chronological*, when your argument follows a change over time; *problem and solution*, when you show a difficulty and then the response; *general to specific*, when you establish a broad claim and then test it in cases; and *weakest to strongest*, when you want the reader's last impression to be your best evidence. Dani used chronology for the first three sections because her thesis was about a change over time, then shifted to argument for the last two.

Hold the building together with *signposting*: sentences that tell the reader where they are and where they are going. The end of each section should look forward: Having shown that the name was already contested in the 1960s, the next section asks what the disputes were about. The start of each section should connect back: These disputes matter for the thesis because they show both communities claiming the name. This may feel clumsy while you write. Readers of long papers are grateful for it.

Two more rules for long arguments. First, address the strongest objection to your thesis somewhere in the body, not in a throwaway line at the end. A reader who has been thinking but what about the other view? for ten pages stops trusting you. Second, keep a running check: after each section, reread the thesis and ask whether that section moved the argument forward. If a section is interesting but does not serve the thesis, cut it or move it to a footnote. Length is not a virtue. Every page must earn its place.

words.d: sentences that tell the reader where the argument has been and where it is going next
arranged in the order events happened in time
the strongest reason a thoughtful reader might reject your thesis, which the paper must address

look.title: Five Rooms, One Building
look.text: Dani's outline: (1) The Czech naming, 1870s. (2) Mexican families arrive, 1950s and 1960s. (3) Two communities, one parish, 1960s and 1970s. (4) Who owns a name? The disputes. (5) What Pilsen means now. Thesis: the name survived because each community found different reasons to keep it.
look.prompt: Which sections are ordered by time and which by argument? Where would you place the strongest objection to Dani's thesis?

check.q: What does the lesson mean by calling each section a room?
choices: Each section should be the same length.
Each section takes up one sub-question and has a clear job.
Each section should have its own thesis.
Sections should be written in separate sittings.
check.why: A reader should enter any section and know what question it answers.

check.q: Where should a long paper address the strongest objection to its thesis?
choices: Only in the title
In a footnote
In a throwaway line at the end
In the body, where it can be answered fully
check.why: Readers who see the objection ignored for ten pages stop trusting the writer.

check.q: A section is interesting but does not move the thesis forward. What does the lesson advise?
choices: Cut it or move it to a footnote
Expand it so it fits
Move it to the introduction
Keep it, since length shows effort
check.why: Every page must earn its place by serving the argument.

lessons.title: MLA and APA Formatting
lessons.mainIdea: MLA and APA are two systems for the same job, letting readers find your sources; MLA cites author and page, APA cites author and year.
reading: Here is one book cited two ways. In *MLA* style: Arredondo, Gabriela F. Mexican Chicago: Race, Identity, and Nation, 1916-39. U of Illinois P, 2008. In *APA* style: Arredondo, G. F. (2008). Mexican Chicago: Race, identity, and nation, 1916-39. University of Illinois Press. Same book, same information, two arrangements. MLA, from the Modern Language Association, is used in English and other humanities courses. APA, from the American Psychological Association, is used in psychology, education, nursing and most social sciences. Your teacher or professor will tell you which one a course expects.

The difference shows most clearly in the *in-text citation*, the short note in parentheses inside your paragraph. MLA gives author and page: (Arredondo 42). APA gives author and year, plus a page number for a quotation: (Arredondo, 2008, p. 42). The reason is a difference in what each field cares about. Literature scholars want to find the exact page. Social scientists want to know how recent the study is. If you name the author in your sentence, leave the name out of the parentheses: Arredondo argues that the community was already forming by 1920 (42) in MLA, or Arredondo (2008) argues in APA.

The list at the end has a different name in each system. In MLA it is Works Cited; in APA it is References. Both are arranged alphabetically by the author's last name, and both use a hanging indent, in which the first line of each entry sits at the margin and the following lines are indented. Titles of books and journals are italicized in both. MLA puts article titles in quotation marks and capitalizes the main words of a title; APA capitalizes only the first word of a title and any proper nouns, and uses no quotation marks around article titles.

A journal article, MLA: Last, First. "Title of Article." Journal Name, vol. 12, no. 3, 2020, pp. 45-67. APA: Last, F. (2020). Title of article. Journal Name, 12(3), 45-67. Do not memorize these patterns; look them up every time in a current handbook or a university writing center's guide, since both systems are revised every few years. What you must memorize is the principle: every source in your text appears in the list, every source in the list appears in your text, and a reader with your list could find every source. Formatting is a courtesy to that reader.

words.d: Modern Language Association style, used in English and the humanities; in-text citations give author and page
American Psychological Association style, used in the social sciences; in-text citations give author and year
the short note in parentheses inside a paragraph that points to an entry in the source list
a format in which the first line of an entry sits at the margin and later lines are indented

look.title: One Paragraph, Two Styles
rows: Words in the MLA in-text citation (Arredondo 42)
Words in the APA in-text citation (Arredondo, 2008, p. 42)
Entries in Dani's Works Cited list
look.prompt: The last two numbers match. What does it mean when a paper's list has more entries than its text cites?

check.q: Which in-text citation is in MLA style?
choices: (Arredondo, 2008)
(Arredondo, 2008, p. 42)
(Arredondo 42)
[Arredondo: 42]
check.why: MLA gives the author's last name and the page number with no comma or year.

check.q: Why does APA put the year in every citation?
choices: Because APA entries have no page numbers
Because it is older than MLA
Because books are cited by year
Because social scientists care how recent a study is
check.why: Author-date citation reflects the field's concern with currency of research.

check.q: What principle does the lesson say to memorize instead of the formatting patterns?
choices: Every source in the text is in the list, every source in the list is in the text, and a reader could find each one.
Always use MLA unless told otherwise.
Italicize everything.
Cite at least twelve sources.
check.why: The purpose of any citation system is that a reader can locate every source.

lessons.title: Quotation, Paraphrase, Summary
lessons.mainIdea: Quote when the exact words matter, paraphrase when the idea matters, summarize when only the gist matters, and cite all three.
reading: Three ways to bring a source into your paper. The source, a sentence from a model article written for this lesson: "The parish did not switch languages so much as add one, holding Czech and Spanish Masses in the same building for nearly two decades." A *quotation* uses those exact words in quotation marks. A *paraphrase* restates the idea in your own words and structure: the church added Spanish services alongside Czech ones rather than replacing them, and the two ran side by side for almost twenty years. A *summary* boils a longer passage or a whole source down to its point: the parish served both communities for years. All three end with a citation.

Choose by asking what the reader needs. Quote when the wording itself is evidence: a striking phrase, a precise definition, a claim you are about to disagree with and want to state fairly. Paraphrase when the idea matters but the wording does not, which is most of the time; paraphrase keeps your paper in your own voice. Summarize when you need a source's overall position in a sentence so you can move on. A paper that is mostly quotations reads like a scrapbook. Aim for far more paraphrase and summary than quotation, and never quote a sentence you could have said more clearly yourself.

A quotation should never stand alone as a sentence. Frame it. Before it, a *signal phrase* names the source and hints at how to take it: As the parish history notes, or One historian argues. After it, a sentence of your own says what the quotation shows and why it matters here. Introduce, quote, explain. Change the quoted words only with visible marks: square brackets for a word you add or alter, an ellipsis of three spaced periods for words you leave out. Never change a quotation so that it says something the source did not mean.

Long quotations get special handling. In MLA, prose longer than four lines of your paper becomes a *block quotation*: start on a new line, indent the whole passage half an inch, and drop the quotation marks. In APA, the block rule starts at forty words. Use blocks rarely; a long quotation shifts work from you to your reader. A real paraphrase, finally, changes both the words and the sentence structure. Swapping a few words while keeping the source's order is patchwriting, and it counts as plagiarism even with a citation. If you cannot restate an idea without the source's wording, you have not yet understood it. Reread until you can.

words.d: a source's exact words, placed in quotation marks and cited
a brief restatement of a source's main point in your own words, with a citation
words that introduce a quotation or paraphrase by naming the source: One historian argues
a long quotation set off on its own indented lines without quotation marks

look.title: Framing a Quotation
look.text: The parish history describes a church that changed by adding rather than replacing: it held "Czech and Spanish Masses in the same building for nearly two decades" (Novak 118). That overlap, not a clean handoff, is the pattern this paper finds throughout the neighborhood's history.
look.cite: model paragraph written for this lesson (the source it cites is invented)
look.prompt: Find the signal phrase, the quotation, the citation and the explaining sentence. What would be lost if the last sentence were cut?

check.q: When does the lesson say to quote rather than paraphrase?
choices: Whenever the source is a scholar
When the exact wording is itself evidence or must be stated fairly before you disagree
Whenever the passage is longer than one sentence
When you are short on words
check.why: Quotation is for wording that matters; most source material should be paraphrased.

check.q: A student swaps a few words in a source sentence, keeps its order, and adds a citation. What is this?
choices: A proper paraphrase
A summary
Patchwriting, which counts as plagiarism
A block quotation
check.why: A true paraphrase changes both the words and the structure; a citation does not excuse copied structure.

check.q: In MLA, when does a prose quotation become a block quotation?
choices: When it is longer than one sentence
At forty words
When it contains a citation
When it runs longer than four lines of your paper
check.why: MLA uses the four-line rule; APA uses forty words.

lessons.title: Drafting in Stages
lessons.mainIdea: Draft the body first, one section at a time, from the outline and the grid; write the introduction last, when you finally know what the paper says.
reading: Dani stared at a blank first page for two evenings, trying to write an opening paragraph for a paper she had not written yet. On the third evening she skipped it. She opened her outline, chose the section she understood best, the arrival of Mexican families, and wrote that. Four pages came in two hours. The rule she discovered is one that experienced writers know: the *introduction* is written last, because you cannot introduce an argument you have not made yet.

Draft in *stages*, one section per sitting. Before each sitting, reread that section's line in the outline and the matching row of your synthesis grid. Then write straight through without stopping to fix sentences, check citations or hunt for the perfect word. Mark gaps with a bracketed note, such as [find the date] or [cite Novak here], and keep moving. A draft's job is to exist. Polishing sentences in a section you may later cut is wasted labor. Stopping to search for a citation breaks the thread of thought, and the thread is the hard part.

Write each body paragraph as a small argument. The first sentence states a *claim* that serves the section's job. The middle brings in evidence from one or more sources, framed and cited. The last sentence or two explains what the evidence shows and connects it to the thesis. Readers of long papers skim first sentences; if your first sentences alone tell the story of the argument, the paper is well built. If your first sentences are all There is another source that says, the paragraphs are stacked, not argued.

When the body exists, write the ending, then the opening. The *conclusion* does not repeat the thesis; it says what the thesis now means, given everything shown, and what remains unanswered. The introduction then does three things in under a page: it opens with the specific scene or question that started you, it states what others have said, and it states your thesis. Dani's final introduction began with the street sign on Eighteenth Street and the question her teacher asked. It was the last page she wrote and the first her reader saw.

words.d: the opening of a paper, written last, that presents the question, the existing views and the thesis
the arguable sentence a paragraph exists to support
the ending, which says what the thesis now means and what remains open, rather than repeating it
one manageable unit of drafting, usually one section written in one sitting

look.title: First Sentences Only
look.text: A reader takes the first sentence of each body paragraph in a draft: 'Czech immigrants named the area for their home city.' 'Another source discusses the churches.' 'There is also a book about the 1960s.' 'Displacement from the Near West Side sent thousands of families west into Pilsen.'
look.prompt: Which first sentences are claims and which are announcements? Rewrite the two weak ones as claims.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to write the introduction last?
choices: Because introductions are graded least
Because you cannot introduce an argument you have not yet made
Because introductions should be short
Because outlines replace introductions
check.why: The opening must present the thesis and the argument's shape, which only exist once the body is drafted.

check.q: While drafting a section, you realize you need a date you do not have. What does the lesson advise?
choices: Stop and search until you find it
Guess and keep going
Mark the gap with a bracketed note and keep writing
Delete the sentence
check.why: A draft's job is to exist; hunting for details breaks the thread of thought.

check.q: What should a conclusion do, according to the lesson?
choices: Repeat the thesis word for word
Introduce a new source
Summarize every section
Say what the thesis now means and what remains unanswered
check.why: The conclusion interprets the argument's result rather than restating it.

lessons.title: Revision With a Reader
lessons.mainIdea: Revision means re-seeing the whole argument through a reader's eyes; a real reader finds the places where the paper made sense only to you.
reading: Dani gave her draft to Marcus, who knew nothing about Pilsen. He read it with a pencil and put a question mark in the margin every time he lost the thread. There were eleven question marks. Three were in one paragraph where she had used the word displacement four times without ever saying what it meant. One was at the top of section four, which began with a quotation and never said why. None of the eleven were places Dani had noticed. She had read the draft six times. She could not see it, because she already knew what it was supposed to say.

That is why *revision* needs a reader. Revision is not proofreading; it is re-seeing the argument as a whole. A reader who does not know your subject is often better than one who does, because the expert fills the gaps in your logic without noticing. Give your reader three questions, not a general request for feedback: Where did you get lost? Where did you stop believing me? What do you think my thesis is? If the reader's answer to the third question is not your thesis, the paper has a problem no proofreading will fix.

Revise from large to small. First the argument: does every section serve the thesis, and is the strongest objection answered? Then the structure: are sections in the best order, and is the signposting clear? Then the paragraphs: does each begin with a claim and end with an explanation? Only then the sentences, and last of all the punctuation and citations. Working in this order keeps you from polishing a paragraph on Tuesday and cutting it on Thursday. Expect to cut. Dani's draft was fourteen pages; her final was eleven and said more.

One tool that catches what readers miss: the *reverse outline*. After the draft exists, write one line for each paragraph stating what it does. Read the list. Paragraphs that do two things need splitting. Two paragraphs that do the same thing need merging. A paragraph whose line you cannot write needs to go. The reverse outline shows you the building you actually built, as opposed to the one you planned, and the two are never the same.

words.d: re-seeing and reworking a whole argument, from thesis to structure to paragraphs, before fixing sentences
a one-line-per-paragraph summary made from a finished draft to reveal its actual structure
the final check for errors in spelling, punctuation, formatting and citations

look.title: Where Marcus Put His Question Marks
look.cite: counted for this lesson from Marcus's marked draft
look.prompt: Which of these problems would proofreading have caught, and which required a reader?

check.q: Why could Dani not see the problems Marcus found?
choices: She already knew what the draft was supposed to say, so she filled gaps without noticing.
She had not read the draft.
Marcus was an expert on Pilsen.
The problems were only spelling errors.
check.why: Writers read their own intentions; a reader sees only what is on the page.

check.q: Which question does the lesson say to ask a reader?
choices: Did you like it?
What do you think my thesis is?
How many pages should it be?
Which font should I use?
check.why: If the reader's version of the thesis is not yours, the argument itself needs work.

check.q: Why revise from large to small?
choices: Because punctuation is unimportant
Because readers only notice structure
So you do not polish paragraphs you will later cut
Because outlines come first
check.why: Fixing argument and structure first prevents wasted work on sentences that will not survive.

lessons.title: Academic Integrity
lessons.mainIdea: Academic integrity means every idea and every phrase that is not yours is marked as someone else's, so a reader can always tell your thinking from your sources.
reading: Two sentences from two student drafts. First: Families followed cousins and coworkers into the neighborhood, building networks that made the move feel less like a leap. Second: Families followed cousins and coworkers into the neighborhood, building networks that made the move feel less like a leap (Novak 121). The words are identical, and they are Novak's. The second sentence has a citation and is still *plagiarism*, because it presents Novak's wording as the student's own. Plagiarism is using someone's words or ideas without making clear that they are theirs. A citation credits the idea. Only quotation marks credit the words.

Plagiarism is rarely a plan. It is usually a shortcut taken at midnight, or a note copied weeks ago without quotation marks and then mistaken for one's own. The defenses are habits you have already learned in this chapter: notes in your own words, with copied phrases marked; page numbers on everything; and a citation for every idea that came from somewhere else, whether quoted, paraphrased or summarized. You do not need to cite *common knowledge*, meaning facts that any general reference would give and that no one could claim as theirs, such as the year Chicago was incorporated. If you are unsure whether something is common knowledge, cite it. No reader has ever complained about an extra citation.

Integrity also covers what you do with sources, not only how you mark them. Do not quote a sentence out of its context so that it seems to say the opposite. Do not cite a source you have not read because it appeared in someone else's bibliography; read it, or cite the source where you found it. Do not invent a page number or a quotation you cannot locate. And do not reuse a paper you wrote for another class without permission; that is *self-plagiarism*, and most schools treat it as a violation. The principle behind all of these is the same: a reader must be able to trust that what you present is what you found.

Writing tools that generate text raise the same question in a new form. If a program produces sentences and you submit them as your own, the words are not yours, and the reader has been misled about who did the thinking. Schools and colleges set their own rules about such tools, and those rules vary and change. Ask what your course allows and follow it exactly. The deeper point holds whatever the rules say: the purpose of a research paper is to make you into someone who can find, weigh and defend evidence. A paper that skips the work skips the point.

words.d: presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, whether on purpose or by accident
facts any general reference would give and no one can claim as theirs; they need no citation
reusing your own earlier work for a new assignment without permission
the honesty that lets a reader trust that your words are yours and your sources are marked

look.title: Bacon on What Writing Does
look.text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
look.prompt: Bacon says writing makes a person exact. How does doing the work of a paper yourself, rather than borrowing it, connect to that claim?

check.q: A student copies a source's sentence exactly and adds a correct citation but no quotation marks. What is this?
choices: A correct paraphrase
A summary
Common knowledge
Plagiarism, because the citation credits the idea but only quotation marks credit the words
check.why: Exact wording presented as your own is plagiarism even with a citation.

check.q: Which fact is common knowledge that needs no citation?
choices: The year Chicago was incorporated as a city
A historian's argument about why families moved
A count from an oral history interview
A quotation from a parish history
check.why: A widely available, uncontested fact needs no citation; arguments and specific findings do.

check.q: You find a useful source listed in another author's bibliography but cannot get a copy. What does the lesson say?
choices: Cite it as if you read it
Cite the source where you found it, or read the original first
Leave it out of the paper and the list
Paraphrase what you imagine it says
check.why: Citing an unread source misleads the reader about what you actually examined.

review.q: Which trait makes a question a research question rather than a lookup?
choices: It has a single correct answer.
It can be answered in one paragraph.
It is arguable: careful readers could reasonably answer it differently.
It is about history.
review.why: Arguability is what turns a topic into a question worth a paper.

review.q: What is the main purpose of a research plan?
choices: To impress the teacher
To break a large task into dated pieces and protect time for revision
To list every source in the library
To replace the outline
review.why: A plan makes the project manageable and keeps revision from being squeezed out.

review.q: A source has named expert authors, was approved by other experts before publication, and lists all its sources. It is best described as what?
choices: A scholarly, peer-reviewed source
A primary source
A blog
Common knowledge
review.why: Expert authorship, peer review and full notes are the marks of a scholarly source.

choices: Summarizing each source in turn
Quoting sources at length
Organizing sources by idea so they answer a question together
Listing sources alphabetically
review.why: Synthesis puts sources in conversation under themes rather than marching through them.

choices: (Arredondo 42)
(Arredondo, 2008, p. 42)
Arredondo, page 42
(2008, Arredondo)
review.why: APA uses author, year and, for quotations, a page number with p.

review.q: Which is the best reason to quote rather than paraphrase?
choices: The passage is long.
You are behind on your word count.
You did not understand the passage.
The exact wording is evidence, or you want to state a view fairly before disagreeing.
review.why: Quote for wording that matters; paraphrase for ideas.

review.q: What is a reverse outline used for?
choices: Planning a paper before drafting
Seeing the structure a draft actually has, paragraph by paragraph
Writing the introduction
Formatting the Works Cited list
review.why: One line per existing paragraph reveals splits, merges and cuts that are needed.

review.q: Why is patchwriting plagiarism even when the source is cited?
choices: Because citations never excuse anything
Because it uses the source's structure and wording as if they were yours
Because it is too short
Because patchwriting has no page number
review.why: A citation credits the idea; a real paraphrase must also change the words and the sentence structure.
